title: Deterministic nanofabrication for engineering nanowire quantum dot devices
authors: Tarun Patel, Matteo Pennacchietti, Greg Holloway, Stephen R. Harrigan, Sayan Gangopadhyay, Anthony Drouin, Megha Jain, Dan Dalacu, Philip J. Poole, Sasan Vosoogh-Grayli, Michael E. Reimer
abstract: Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are a leading platform for realising bright, wavelength-tunable sources of single and entangled photon pairs for photonic quantum technologies. Site-selected nanowire quantum dots (NWQDs) are a promising platform for fabricating such photonic devices in a scalable manner. However, implementing additional structures around the photonic nanowire while maintaining its vertical growth geometry has remained a challenge. In this work, we develop a deterministic pick-and-place technique to conduct a vertical-to-vertical transfer of NWQDs from the growth substrate to arbitrary templates. Using this transfer technique, we enhance the photon extraction efficiency to 75% by implementing a bottom gold mirror and tune the emission wavelength by 3.6 GHz via implementing electrostatic gates around the QD. Importantly, we measure low-multiphoton probability (g^(2)(0) = 0.002) and high indistinguishability (>80% for +/-100 ps) of the QD emission after the transfer process, yielding high-quality devices. These results demonstrate the repeatability and versatility of the developed transfer technique, which is an enabling step towards scalable single and entangled photon sources.
summary: The authors present a novel, deterministic pick-and-place technique to transfer nanowire quantum dots (NWQDs) while preserving their high optical quality. By combining this transfer method with bottom mirror structures and electrostatic gates, they demonstrate the creation of highly efficient, tunable single-photon sources crucial for quantum technologies.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is developing a scalable, deterministic method to engineer nanowire quantum dot (NWQD) devices by transferring them while maintaining their critical vertical growth geometry.
main_result: The developed pick-and-place transfer technique successfully preserves high optical quality, enabling the integration of bottom mirrors for 75% photon extraction efficiency and electrostatic gates for wavelength tuning.
method: The work combines a deterministic, gas-assisted pick-and-place transfer technique with advanced optical characterization (PL, lifetime, HBT measurements) and theoretical modeling (FDTD simulations).
model_or_system: The system involves semiconductor NWQDs (e.g., InAsP in InP) integrated into photonic nanowires. The process involves transferring these QDs from a growth substrate to arbitrary templates, such as those incorporating bottom gold mirrors or gate electrodes.
key_observables: Low-multiphoton probability ($g_2(0)=0.002$), high indistinguishability ($>80\%$), enhanced photon extraction efficiency (up to 75%), and measurable spectral tuning via gates.
important_parameters: The transfer process itself, the efficiency enhancement factor (e.g., 1.58 Purcell enhancement), and the achievable wavelength tunability ($\sim 3.6 	ext{ GHz}$).
main_assumptions: The transfer process is assumed to preserve the quantum optical properties of the QD emission, and theoretical models rely on specific coupling strengths and modal reflectivities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the deterministic pick-and-place transfer steps (detachment, gluing, placement) and show PL spectra before and after transfer, confirming spectral and linewidth preservation.
paper_structure: The paper details the development of the deterministic transfer technique, followed by comprehensive optical characterization demonstrating enhanced light collection efficiency using bottom mirrors, and finally, tuning capabilities using electrostatic gates.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of integrating quantum emitters into complex photonic circuits, which is foundational for scalable quantum light sources and quantum networking components.
